title: OOP Fundamentals
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Think of OOP like organizing a hospital into Doctors, Patients, and Pharmacy—each owns its own data and responsibilities rather than one giant global spreadsheet.
simpleExplanation: OOP is a programming paradigm where we organize software around **objects**—bundles of data (state) and functions (behavior)—rather than separate functions and global/loose data. In procedural programming, as a codebase grows, any function can accidentally modify shared data, making bugs hard to trace. OOP groups related data with the exact functions allowed to touch it, making large systems modular, reusable, and easier to maintain.
technicalExplanation:
Procedural code separates data structures (`struct`) from algorithms (free functions). OOP binds them into classes, enforcing invariants via access control (`private`/`public`) and enabling extensibility via inheritance and polymorphism. Note that C++ is a *multi-paradigm* language (supports procedural, OOP, and generic programming), not purely OOP like Smalltalk or Java.

In C++, encapsulation uses `private`/`protected` access specifiers; abstraction uses headers, abstract classes (`= 0`), and clean public APIs; inheritance uses `: public Base`; polymorphism uses function/operator overloading (compile-time) and `virtual` functions (runtime).

C++ follows the **"zero-overhead principle"** (*you don't pay for what you don't use*). A class with only non-virtual methods has the exact same `sizeof` as a C `struct` with the same data members. Virtual dispatch costs: (a) 1 `vptr` (usually 8 bytes on 64-bit) per object, (b) 1 vtable per polymorphic class (not per object), (c) indirect branch through vtable (harder for CPU branch predictor and compiler inlining unless devirtualized).

interviewTraps: *"Is OOP always better than procedural programming? When would you avoid OOP?"* (Answer: Small utility scripts, tight performance-critical loops needing Data-Oriented Design for CPU cache locality, or pure mathematical pipelines.)

*"Can you achieve abstraction without inheritance? Can you have encapsulation without classes?"* (Yes: a `.h` file exposing free functions while hiding `static` helper state in `.cpp` achieves module-level encapsulation/abstraction in C.)

*"When can the compiler eliminate virtual call overhead automatically?"* (Devirtualization: when the concrete type is known statically, e.g., calling via a value object `Circle c; c.draw();` or using `final`.)

Mixing up **Encapsulation** ("data hiding + bundling") and **Abstraction** ("design-level hiding of implementation details behind an interface").
Thinking every member function is stored inside every object in memory, or thinking every class automatically has a vtable.

title: Class & Objects
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: A Class is an architectural blueprint for a house; Objects are the actual houses built on plots of land from that blueprint.
simpleExplanation: A **class** is a user-defined blueprint or data type that describes what properties (variables) and behaviors (functions) something will have. An **object** is a real instance created in memory from that blueprint. Defining a class does **not** allocate memory for its non-static members; memory is allocated only when you instantiate an object (except `static` data members, which exist once per program in static storage).
technicalExplanation:
The compiler uses the class definition to compute member offsets, alignment, padding, and `sizeof(ClassName)`. When you write `Student s;`, memory of `sizeof(Student)` bytes is reserved on the stack (or heap via `new` / `std::make_unique`).

Wait—there is a famous exception! **Empty Base Optimization (EBO):** If an empty class is used as a *base class* (`class Derived : public Empty { int x; };`), the compiler does **not** have to allocate that 1 byte separately; `sizeof(Derived)` is typically just `sizeof(int)` = 4 bytes! (Also in C++20, `[[no_unique_address]]` extends this to data members.)

```cpp
  class BadLayout  { char a; double b; char c; }; // 1 + 7(pad) + 8 + 1 + 7(pad) = 24 bytes
  class GoodLayout { double b; char a; char c; }; // 8 + 1 + 1 + 6(pad) = 16 bytes
  ```
  The total size of a class must also be a multiple of its strictest member alignment so arrays of that class stay aligned.
definitions: A **class** is a user-defined blueprint or data type that describes what properties (variables) and behaviors (functions) something will have. An **object** is a real instance created in memory from that blueprint. Defining a class does **not** allocate memory for its non-static members; memory is allocated only when you instantiate an object (except `static` data members, which exist once per program in static storage).

Because C++ requires every distinct object to have a **unique memory address**. If an empty class had size `0`, then two consecutive objects in an array `Empty arr[2];` would sit at the exact same address (`&arr[0] == &arr[1]`), breaking pointer arithmetic and object identity. So the compiler inserts 1 dummy byte.

interviewTraps: *"Where in memory can an object live?"* (Stack for local automatic objects, Heap/Free Store for `new`, Data/BSS segment for global/static objects.)
*"What happens to `sizeof(Empty)` if you add one `virtual` function inside `Empty`?"* (It jumps from 1 byte to `sizeof(void*)`—typically 8 bytes on 64-bit—because of the `vptr`.)

*"Does C++ allow the compiler to reorder members inside a class automatically to save space?"* (No, within the same access specifier, members must be laid out in declaration order. Across different access specifiers like `private`/`public`, the standard permits reordering, though most compilers preserve declaration order.)

Adding up member sizes (`1 + 8 + 1 = 10`) and claiming `sizeof(BadLayout) == 10`.

title: Access Modifiers
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Access modifiers are security badges: public is the lobby, protected is staff-only + branch offices, private is the vault.
simpleExplanation:
Access modifiers control *who* can access a class's members:
  - `public`: Accessible from anywhere (inside the class, derived classes, and outside code like `main()`).
  - `private`: Accessible only inside the same class (and its `friend`s). Not accessible even by derived classes.
  - `protected`: Accessible inside the same class, its `friend`s, and **derived classes**, but hidden from outside code.
technicalExplanation:
In a `class`, the default access modifier is `private`. In a `struct`, the default access modifier is `public`.

At compile time, `basePtr` has type `Base*`, where `func()` is `public`, so the compiler allows the call. At runtime, vtable dispatch jumps to `Derived::func()`. Conversely, if `Base::func()` is `private`, calling `derivedPtr->func()` fails to compile if `Derived` didn't re-declare it `public`—and even if `Base::func()` is `private virtual`, `Derived` *can* still override it (this is the famous **Non-Virtual Interface / NVI** pattern!).
definitions: Access modifiers control *who* can access a class's members:

**Yes!** In C++, access control is **class-based**, not object-based. Any member function of class `A` can access the `private` members of *any* object of class `A` passed into it—which is exactly how copy constructors and `operator=` work!
interviewTraps: *"Is `private` checked at compile time or runtime?"* (Strictly at **compile time**! Zero runtime cost.)
*"Why would copy constructors break if access were object-based?"* (Because `Box(const Box& other)` could not read `other.width` without calling getters for every field.)

*"What is the NVI (Non-Virtual Interface) idiom and why do senior C++ engineers use `private virtual`?"* (A public non-virtual method in Base acts as a template: checks preconditions, calls a `private virtual` hook overridden by Derived, checks postconditions.)

---
commonMistakes: Thinking `protected` means "accessible from other classes in the same file" (that's closer to Java's package-private, which C++ does not have).
Saying *"No, `other.width` is private to `other` so `this` cannot read it."*
Assuming `private` functions cannot be overridden in C++ (`private virtual` CAN be overridden in derived classes, even though derived classes cannot call `Base::func()`).

title: Encapsulation
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Encapsulation is a medicine capsule: it seals the active ingredients inside and gives you a safe outer dosage interface.
simpleExplanation: Encapsulation is bundling data and the methods that operate on that data into a single class while **restricting direct external access** to the internal state. If all data were `public`, any caller could put an object into an invalid state (e.g., `bankAccount.balance = -10000;` or `date.month = 99;`), and changing the internal representation later would break all external code.
technicalExplanation:
Encapsulation preserves **class invariants** (rules that must always remain true for an object to be valid, like `size <= capacity`).

Friendship is explicitly granted *by* the class owning the private data (it cannot be claimed from outside). Thus the class author still controls the boundary of encapsulation.
definitions: Encapsulation is bundling data and the methods that operate on that data into a single class while **restricting direct external access** to the internal state. If all data were `public`, any caller could put an object into an invalid state (e.g., `bankAccount.balance = -10000;` or `date.month = 99;`), and changing the internal representation later would break all external code.

Even if a variable is `private`, if a `public` getter returns `int&` or `int*` (or a non-const reference to an internal `std::vector`), outside code now holds a direct handle to your private memory and can mutate it freely, bypassing all validation!
interviewTraps: *"If a class has getters and setters for every private variable, how is it any better than public variables?"* (Only slightly better if setters validate inputs or log/lock; otherwise, it's anemic design that breaks encapsulation.)

*"What if a `const` getter returns a `const` reference, and the caller keeps that reference after the object is destroyed?"* (Dangling reference -> Undefined Behavior! Sometimes returning by value or `std::string_view` with care is safer.)

*"Give a concrete C++ case where `friend` is practically unavoidable."* (`operator<<` for `std::ostream`, where the left operand is `std::ostream&`—a class you don't own—so it cannot be a member function of your class.)

---
commonMistakes: Thinking making every field `private` and blindly adding trivial getters and setters for every field is "good encapsulation." (Trivial setters expose raw state anyway; real encapsulation exposes *behavioral* methods like `withdraw()` or `resize()`.)
Returning `T&` from getters thinking *"I wrote `private:` so it's encapsulated."*
Blindly repeating *"Never use `friend`, it breaks encapsulation."*

title: Abstraction
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Abstraction is a car's dashboard: steering wheel and pedals hide fuel injection, spark timing, and ABS hydraulics.
simpleExplanation: Abstraction means showing only the **essential features** to the user and hiding unnecessary internal complexity. Think of driving a car: you interact with a simple interface—steering wheel, accelerator, brake—without needing to know fuel injection timing, piston firing order, or ABS hydraulic logic.
technicalExplanation:
In C++, abstraction exists at multiple levels:
  - **Header/Implementation split:** `.hpp` declares what functions exist; `.cpp` hides how they work.
  - **Abstract classes / Interfaces:** `PaymentGateway` declares `virtual bool pay(double) = 0;` while hiding `StripeGateway` or `UPI` network protocols.

Benefits: faster compile times (compilation firewall) and ABI stability (you can modify `Impl` internals in a shared library without breaking client binaries). Note that the destructor `~Widget()` must be declared in `.hpp` and defined in `.cpp` (even as `= default`) where `Impl` is a complete type, otherwise `std::unique_ptr<Impl>` fails to compile.
definitions: Abstraction means showing only the **essential features** to the user and hiding unnecessary internal complexity. Think of driving a car: you interact with a simple interface—steering wheel, accelerator, brake—without needing to know fuel injection timing, piston firing order, or ABS hydraulic logic.

Abstraction is the **design goal** (*what* the user sees), and Encapsulation is the **implementation mechanism** (*how* we hide the internals so users can't touch them). For example, `std::vector` abstracts a dynamic array (`push_back`, `size`), and encapsulates its raw `T* data`, `size_t capacity`, and `size_t count` as `private` so you can't corrupt the pointer.
interviewTraps: *"Can you have abstraction without abstract classes?"* (Yes! `std::sort` or `std::vector::push_back` provides huge abstraction—you don't know introsort pivots or buffer reallocation formulas—without using virtual functions.)

*"If I put all implementation details in a `private` helper method, is that abstraction or encapsulation?"* (Both: hiding helper access with `private` is encapsulation; exposing only high-level public operations like `checkout()` is abstraction.)

*"What is the runtime trade-off of PIMPL?"* (One extra heap allocation per object and one extra pointer dereference per member access.)

title: Constructors
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: A constructor is the setup checklist run the instant a new phone is unboxed so it never starts in a broken state.
simpleExplanation:
A constructor is a special member function automatically called when an object is created, used to initialize the object's data members and establish valid starting invariants. It has the **exact same name as the class** and **no return type** (not even `void`).  
  Main types:
  1. **Default constructor:** Can be called with zero arguments (`A()` or `A(int x = 0)`).
  2. **Parameterized constructor:** Accepts arguments to initialize the object (`A(int x)`).
  3. **Copy constructor:** Initializes an object from another object of the same class (`A(const A& other)`).
  4. **Move constructor (C++11):** Transfers resources from a temporary/rvalue object (`A(A&& other) noexcept`).
technicalExplanation:
Even for normal members like `std::string name;`, initializing `: name(n)` calls only the copy/move constructor once, whereas `name = n;` inside the body default-constructs an empty string first and then calls `operator=` (wasteful double work).

In C++11+, constructors with multiple parameters can also be `explicit` to prevent implicit brace-initialization like `return {1, 2};` from converting silently.
definitions: A constructor is a special member function automatically called when an object is created, used to initialize the object's data members and establish valid starting invariants. It has the **exact same name as the class** and **no return type** (not even `void`).

A member initializer list (`Point(int x, int y) : x_(x), y_(y) {}`) initializes members *directly* before the constructor body begins, instead of default-constructing them first and overwriting them inside `{}`.
interviewTraps: *"Can a constructor be `virtual`?"* (No—see Q6.3.)
*"What happens if `: b(a), a(10)` is written when `int a;` is declared after `int b;`?"* (`b` is initialized first using uninitialized garbage `a` -> **Undefined Behavior**!)

*"If a class needs a virtual-like creation mechanism (cloning an object through a base pointer), how do you achieve it?"* (Use the **Virtual Constructor / Clone Idiom**: `virtual std::unique_ptr<Base> clone() const = 0;`.)

---
commonMistakes: Saying *"Constructors return `void`"* or *"If I write a parameterized constructor, the compiler still gives me a default constructor."* (False: defining *any* custom constructor suppresses the compiler-generated default constructor unless you explicitly write `A() = default;`.)
Thinking members are initialized in the order written in the initializer list! **Trap:** They are ALWAYS initialized in the order they are **declared inside the class**!
Writing `Buffer b = 10;` and not realizing why it fails when `Buffer(int)` is `explicit` (copy-initialization rejects `explicit` constructors; direct-initialization `Buffer b(10);` works).

questions.question: What is a Member Initializer List, and when is it **mandatory** instead of assigning inside the constructor body?

  1. `const` data members (cannot be assigned inside body).
  2. Reference data members (`int& ref;` must be bound at initialization).
  3. Member objects of classes that have **no default constructor**.
  4. Calling a specific **base class constructor** (`Derived(int a) : Base(a) {}`).

questions.question: Why can't a constructor be `virtual`, `const`, or `static`? And what is `explicit` on a constructor?
questions.answer:
- **Not `virtual`:** Virtual dispatch relies on the object's `vptr` (virtual pointer) pointing to the vtable. While a constructor is running, the object isn't fully constructed yet—in fact, the constructor *sets up* the `vptr`! Also, you always state the exact type when constructing (`new Derived()`).
  - **Not `const`:** A constructor's whole job is to initialize (write to) the object's members; `const` semantics only apply *after* construction finishes.
  - **Not `static`:** A constructor initializes a *specific* object (`this`), whereas `static` functions have no `this` pointer.
  - **`explicit`:** Prevents accidental **implicit conversions** by single-argument constructors. For example, if `Buffer(int size)` is not `explicit`, calling `printBuffer(10)` silently constructs a temporary `Buffer(10)`! Marking it `explicit Buffer(int size)` stops that silent conversion.
questions.technicalExplanation: In C++11+, constructors with multiple parameters can also be `explicit` to prevent implicit brace-initialization like `return {1, 2};` from converting silently.

title: Copy Constructor
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Copy constructor is clicking 'Duplicate Document'—creating a brand-new independent file from an existing one.
simpleExplanation:
A copy constructor creates a **new** object as an exact duplicate of an existing object of the same class: `MyClass(const MyClass& other)`.  
  It is called in 4 common places (when elision doesn't optimize it away):
  1. Initializing a new object from an existing one: `MyClass b = a;` or `MyClass b(a);`
  2. Passing an object **by value** to a function: `void f(MyClass obj);`
  3. Returning an object **by value** from a function (when NRVO/RVO doesn't elide it).
  4. Constructing elements inside containers (e.g., `std::vector::push_back(obj)`).
technicalExplanation:
Using `const T&` avoids copying AND allows binding to both lvalues (`a`) and temporary rvalues (`MyClass(5)`), as well as `const` objects. (You *can* write `T(T&)` without `const`, though it breaks copying `const` objects and temporaries.)

Before C++11, people made the copy constructor `private` without a body (which caused a confusing linker error if called by a friend/member). `= delete` gives a clean, immediate compile-time diagnostic.
definitions: A copy constructor creates a **new** object as an exact duplicate of an existing object of the same class: `MyClass(const MyClass& other)`.

If the copy constructor took its argument by value—`MyClass(MyClass other)`—then calling the copy constructor would have to pass `other` **by value**. Passing by value *requires calling the copy constructor* to copy the argument into `other`, which again needs the copy constructor... causing **infinite recursion**! That's why C++ makes passing by value in a copy constructor a **compile-time error**.
interviewTraps: *"Wait—if I write `MyClass b = func();`, why might the copy constructor NOT print anything in C++17?"* (**Guaranteed Copy Elision** in C++17 for prvalues, and NRVO for named local variables!)

*"What happens if you inherit from a base class and write a custom copy constructor in `Derived`, without calling `Base(other)` in the initializer list?"* (The compiler calls `Base()` default constructor instead of `Base(other)`, so the base part of `Derived` is NOT copied—a subtle bug!)

*"If you mark `MyClass(const MyClass&) = delete;`, does the compiler still generate a move constructor?"* (No! Declaring any copy operation suppresses automatic generation of move operations too.)

---
commonMistakes: Confusing `MyClass b = a;` (calls **Copy Constructor** because `b` is being *born*) with `b = a;` when `b` already exists (calls **Copy Assignment Operator**).
Saying *"Passing by value causes infinite recursion at runtime."* (No! The C++ compiler rejects `T(T other)` at **compile time**.)
Thinking `= delete` is only for constructors, or thinking adding a move constructor keeps the implicit copy constructor active.

title: Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Shallow copy shares one Google Docs link (edits collide); Deep copy saves a separate local copy on your own drive.
simpleExplanation:
- **Shallow Copy:** Copies member values bit-for-bit (or member-by-member). If an object holds a raw pointer `int* ptr`, only the **memory address** is copied—both objects now point to the exact same heap memory.
  - **Deep Copy:** Allocates **separate memory** for the new object and copies the actual data stored at that address, so the two objects are completely independent.
technicalExplanation: Without the custom copy constructor and `operator=`, `IntBox b = a;` copies `a.data` pointer address into `b.data`. Modifying `*b.data = 99` mutates `*a.data`, and destruction double-frees.

interviewTraps: *"What happens when two shallow-copied objects owning a raw pointer go out of scope?"* (The first destructor calls `delete ptr`, and the second destructor calls `delete ptr` on the same already-freed address -> **Double Free**, which is **Undefined Behavior** and usually crashes!)
*"Why did we allocate `new int(*other.data)` BEFORE calling `delete data` in `operator=`?"* (Strong exception safety: if `new` throws `std::bad_alloc`, `this->data` isn't left dangling!)

*"What problem happens if two `std::shared_ptr` objects point to each other?"* (A **cyclic reference**, where the reference count never drops to 0, causing a memory leak—solved using `std::weak_ptr`.)

---
commonMistakes: Saying *"Shallow copy is always bad."* (If your class has no raw owning pointers—only `int`, `double`, `std::string`, `std::vector`—the default memberwise copy does the exact right thing: `std::string` and `std::vector` already deep-copy themselves!)
Writing a deep copy constructor (`IntBox(const IntBox&)`) but forgetting `operator=` (or vice versa), leaving half the bug alive!
Trying to manually track reference counts with raw pointers instead of `std::shared_ptr` (easy to get thread-safety and exception-safety wrong).

questions.question: When is sharing memory (shallow pointer copy) actually desired, and how does modern C++ do it safely without double-free bugs?
questions.answer:
Sometimes multiple objects legitimately need to **share ownership** of the same heap resource (e.g., an immutable large texture or config shared across threads/objects), OR observe a resource without owning it. In modern C++:
  - Use **`std::shared_ptr<T>`** for safe shared ownership (it uses reference counting, destroying the resource only when the last owner dies).
  - Use a **non-owning raw pointer / reference / `std::weak_ptr<T>`** when an object only observes without deleting.

title: Destructor
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: A destructor is the cleanup crew automatically locked to run the moment you exit a hotel room—returning keys and turning off lights.
simpleExplanation: A destructor is a special member function prefixed with `~` (e.g., `~FileHandler()`) that runs automatically right before an object is destroyed, used to release resources (heap memory, file handles, sockets, mutex locks). It takes **no parameters**, has **no return type**, and **cannot be overloaded** (at most one destructor per class).
technicalExplanation:
- Automatic (stack) objects: destroyed when control leaves their `{}` block (even if an exception is thrown—stack unwinding!).
  - Dynamic (heap) objects: destroyed when `delete ptr` (or `std::unique_ptr` goes out of scope) runs.
  - Static/Global objects: destroyed after `main()` returns, in reverse order of construction.

Since C++11, all destructors are implicitly **`noexcept(true)`** by default. If an uncaught exception escapes a `noexcept` destructor, `std::terminate()` is invoked immediately. Best practice: catch and log errors inside the destructor instead of letting exceptions escape.
definitions: A destructor is a special member function prefixed with `~` (e.g., `~FileHandler()`) that runs automatically right before an object is destroyed, used to release resources (heap memory, file handles, sockets, mutex locks). It takes **no parameters**, has **no return type**, and **cannot be overloaded** (at most one destructor per class).

Suppose an exception is already thrown, and C++ is destroying local stack objects during **stack unwinding**. If one of those destructors *also* throws an uncaught exception while another exception is active, C++ doesn't know which exception to propagate and immediately calls **`std::terminate()`**, crashing the program!
interviewTraps: *"Can a destructor be called explicitly like `obj.~MyClass()`?"* (Yes, only in rare low-level cases like **placement `new`**; calling it on a normal stack variable causes double-destruction when the scope ends -> UB.)

*"How should a class communicate a `close()` failure if the destructor cannot throw?"* (Provide an explicit `close()` method that *can* throw for callers who care, and have `~FileCloser()` silently swallow/log any remaining error if not already closed.)

*"Can a class with a `private` destructor be inherited from?"* (No—unless the derived class is a `friend`, because the derived destructor must invoke the base destructor!)

---
commonMistakes: Thinking a destructor deletes the object's stack memory itself. (No! The destructor cleans up *resources owned by* the object; stack/heap reclamation happens around it.)
Writing `throw std::runtime_error(...)` inside `~FileCloser()` if `fclose` fails.
Assuming a class with a `private` destructor cannot be instantiated at all. (`MyClass* p = new MyClass();` compiles fine! You just need a public `destroy()` or `friend` to delete it.)

  2. **Singleton pattern** (prevents accidental deletion of the static/singleton instance).

title: Constructor & Destructor Execution Order
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Construction builds a building bottom-up (foundation/Base first, then rooms/Members, then roof/Derived); destruction tears down top-down.
simpleExplanation:
- **Construction:** Base first, then Derived (`Base()` -> `Derived()`). Because `Derived` depends on `Base` being ready first (just like building a house's ground floor before the first floor).
  - **Destruction:** Exact reverse (`~Derived()` -> `~Base()`). Because `Derived` might still use `Base` data during its cleanup.
technicalExplanation: When `Base::Base()` is running, `Derived` members haven't even been initialized yet—calling `Derived::log()` would read garbage memory! So C++ dynamically sets the object's `vptr` to `Base`'s vtable during `Base::Base()`. Similarly, during `Base::~Base()`, `Derived` has *already been destroyed*, so the `vptr` is reset back to `Base`'s vtable.
definitions: - **Construction:** Base first, then Derived (`Base()` -> `Derived()`). Because `Derived` depends on `Base` being ready first (just like building a house's ground floor before the first floor).
C++ guarantees this strict 4-step construction order:
interviewTraps: *"What if `Derived` also has a member object `Engine engine;` inside it?"* (Construction: `Base()` -> `Engine()` -> `Derived()`. Destruction: `~Derived()` -> `~Engine()` -> `~Base()`.)

*"What happens if a constructor throws an exception halfway through constructing member #2?"* (Members #1 and base classes that *already finished* constructing are destroyed automatically, while the destructor of the enclosing class itself does **not** run because the object was never fully born!)

*"What happens if a constructor calls a non-virtual helper function, which in turn calls a **pure virtual** function (`= 0`)?"* (**Undefined Behavior!** Usually crashes at runtime with *"pure virtual method called"*.)

---
commonMistakes: Writing `Derived` destructor order as `~Base()` then `~Derived()`.

Thinking multiple inheritance runs base constructors in the order they appear in the member initializer list (`Derived() : B(), A()` when declared `class Derived : public A, public B`). **Trap:** Declaration order (`A`, then `B`) always wins!

Expecting runtime polymorphism inside constructors (a classic Java/C# habit that works differently—and dangerously—in those languages, whereas C++ protects you by slicing the dynamic type to the currently constructing/destructing class).

questions.question: In single inheritance (`Derived` inherits from `Base`), what is the order of constructor and destructor calls?
questions.answer:
- **Construction:** Base first, then Derived (`Base()` -> `Derived()`). Because `Derived` depends on `Base` being ready first (just like building a house's ground floor before the first floor).
  - **Destruction:** Exact reverse (`~Derived()` -> `~Base()`). Because `Derived` might still use `Base` data during its cleanup.
questions.commonMistake: Writing `Derived` destructor order as `~Base()` then `~Derived()`.
questions.followUp: *"What if `Derived` also has a member object `Engine engine;` inside it?"* (Construction: `Base()` -> `Engine()` -> `Derived()`. Destruction: `~Derived()` -> `~Engine()` -> `~Base()`.)

questions.question: If a class has both base classes and member objects, what is the exact guaranteed construction order?
questions.answer:
C++ guarantees this strict 4-step construction order:
  1. **Virtual base classes** (top-down, left-to-right in the inheritance hierarchy).
  2. **Direct non-virtual base classes** (left-to-right as listed after `:`).
  3. **Non-static data members** (in the **order declared inside the class**, NOT the order in the initializer list).
  4. **The constructor body `{ ... }`** of the class itself.  
  Destruction is always the **exact mirror image** (4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1).

So C++ dynamically sets the object's `vptr` to `Base`'s vtable during `Base::Base()`. Similarly, during `Base::~Base()`, `Derived` has *already been destroyed*, so the `vptr` is reset back to `Base`'s vtable.

*"What happens if a constructor calls a non-virtual helper function, which in turn calls a **pure virtual** function (`= 0`)?"* (**Undefined Behavior!** Usually crashes at runtime with *"pure virtual method called"*.)

title: `this` Pointer
chapterTitle: Chapter 1: OOP Foundations, Constructors & Object Lifetime
analogy: Every hotel room shares the same room-service handbook (member function), while the room keycard (`this`) tells staff which room called.

analogy: Non-static members are personal wallets; a `static` member is the shared bank vault belonging to the whole branch.
simpleExplanation:

technicalExplanation:

title: Types of Inheritance
analogy: Inheritance types describe family trees: chain (multilevel), siblings (hierarchical), two parents (multiple), or diamond (hybrid).

  3. **Hierarchical:** Multiple classes (`B`, `C`) inherit from one `A`.
  4. **Multiple:** One class `C` inherits from two or more classes (`A` and `B`).

title: Inheritance Access Modes
analogy: Inheritance access modes act like a permission ceiling: `private` inheritance hides the base badge from outsiders.

  - **`protected` inheritance:** `Base`'s `public` and `protected` -> both become `protected` in `Derived`.
  - **`private` inheritance:** `Base`'s `public` and `protected` -> both become `private` in `Derived`.

`private` inheritance means **"is-implemented-in-terms-of"**, NOT "is-a". Outside callers cannot convert `Derived*` to `Base*`. Usually **composition** (putting `Base` as a `private` member variable) is cleaner and preferred.

title: Function Overloading
analogy: Function overloading is one word like 'open' meaning different things depending on whether you pass a Door, a File, or a Bottle.
simpleExplanation: Function overloading lets you define multiple functions with the **same name** in the **same scope**, as long as their **parameter lists differ** (in number of parameters, parameter types, or parameter order). It is an example of **compile-time polymorphism**.
technicalExplanation:
The compiler decides which overload to call at compile time via **overload resolution** (Exact Match > Promotion > Standard Conversion > User-Defined Conversion > Ellipsis `...`).

Compiler name lookup stops at the innermost scope (`Derived`) as soon as it finds *any* match for the name `log`, before overload resolution even starts!
definitions: Function overloading lets you define multiple functions with the **same name** in the **same scope**, as long as their **parameter lists differ** (in number of parameters, parameter types, or parameter order). It is an example of **compile-time polymorphism**.

Because the linker needs unique symbol names for each function, the C++ compiler encodes the function name + parameter types into a unique internal name (e.g., `print(int)` -> `_Z5printi`, `print(double)` -> `_Z5printd`). That process is **Name Mangling**.
interviewTraps: *"Can you overload `main()`? Can you overload constructors?"* (Constructors: yes! `main()`: technically prohibited by the C++ standard as a special reserved entry point.)
*"Why do we write `extern "C"` when calling C functions from C++?"* (To disable C++ name mangling so the linker finds the plain C symbol name!)

*"Does this name hiding happen even if `Base::log(int)` is `virtual`?"* (Yes! Declaring `void log(string)` in `Derived` still hides `Base::log(int)` unless `using Base::log;` is written.)

questions.question: Explain **Name Mangling**, and explain which differences in parameters do and do NOT create valid overloads.

  - `void f(int x)` vs `void f(const int x)` (top-level `const` on pass-by-value is ignored!)
  - `void f(int*)` vs `void f(int[])` (array decays to pointer—same type!)

title: Runtime Polymorphism
analogy: Runtime polymorphism is pressing 'Play' on a universal remote: TV, Speaker, or Projector responds differently depending on the device connected.
simpleExplanation:
Runtime polymorphism allows calling a method through a `Base` pointer or reference and having C++ decide **at runtime** which `Derived` version to execute based on the actual object stored there.  
  Three required ingredients in C++:
  1. **Inheritance** (`Derived` inherits `public`ly from `Base`).
  2. **`virtual` function** in `Base` overridden by `Derived`.
  3. Calling via a **Base pointer (`Base*`) or Base reference (`Base&`)** (NOT a `Base` value!).
definitions: Runtime polymorphism allows calling a method through a `Base` pointer or reference and having C++ decide **at runtime** which `Derived` version to execute based on the actual object stored there.
*(Note: The C++ standard doesn't mandate vtables, though every major compiler implements runtime polymorphism this way.)*
interviewTraps: *"Why doesn't C++ make all functions `virtual` by default like Java?"* (C++ philosophy: *"You don't pay for what you don't use."* Virtual calls cost a `vptr` per object and prevent some inlining.)

*"How many extra bytes does adding a second `virtual` function add to `sizeof(Obj)`?"* (Zero extra bytes on the object! The object still holds only **one `vptr`**; the class's single vtable simply gets one extra slot.)

*"If you see `if (dynamic_cast<Dog*>(a)) ... else if (dynamic_cast<Cat*>(a)) ...` in a codebase, what OOP smell is that?"* (Violation of Open/Closed Principle and Polymorphism—the behavior should be a virtual method on `Animal`.)

questions.question: Explain **vtable** and **vptr** simply—how does C++ actually implement dynamic dispatch under the hood?

*(Note: The C++ standard doesn't mandate vtables, though every major compiler implements runtime polymorphism this way.)*  
  - **vtable (Virtual Table):** A hidden lookup array of function pointers created **once per polymorphic class** (in read-only memory). It maps each `virtual` function slot to the concrete function address for that class.
  - **vptr (Virtual Pointer):** A hidden pointer stored **inside every object** of that class, automatically set by the constructor to point to that class's vtable.  
  When you call `ptr->draw()`: at runtime, the CPU follows `ptr->vptr`, looks up the `draw` slot in the vtable, and jumps to the right function (`Circle::draw` or `Square::draw`)!

questions.question: When should you use `dynamic_cast`, how does it work (RTTI), and what happens when it fails on pointers vs references?

  - **Requirement:** `Base` **must be polymorphic** (must have at least one `virtual` function), otherwise `dynamic_cast` won't even compile!
  - **Failure on Pointer:** `dynamic_cast<Derived*>(basePtr)` returns **`nullptr`** if the object isn't actually a `Derived`.
  - **Failure on Reference:** Since a reference cannot be null, `dynamic_cast<Derived&>(baseRef)` throws **`std::bad_cast`**!

title: Operator Overloading
analogy: Operator overloading teaches `+` or `<<` how to add two Complex numbers or print a Matrix naturally like built-in `int`s.
simpleExplanation:

  2. `.` (Member access)

  4. `?:` (Ternary conditional)

title: Composition vs Aggregation
analogy: Composition: a Heart belongs to one Body and dies with it. Aggregation: a Student belongs to a Club but survives if the Club closes.
simpleExplanation:
Both represent a **"has-a"** (whole–part) relationship, but differ in **ownership and lifetime**:
  - **Composition (Strong "has-a" / "part-of"):** The part **cannot exist independently** of the whole. When the whole dies, the part dies with it. Example: `House` has `Room`s, or `Car` owns its `Engine` (`Engine engine_;` by value or `std::unique_ptr<Engine>`).
  - **Aggregation (Weak "has-a"):** The part **can exist independently** of the whole and may be shared. When the whole is destroyed, the part survives. Example: `Department` has `Professor`s (`std::vector<Professor*>` or `std::weak_ptr<Professor>`).

interviewTraps: *"Why does the C++ community say 'Prefer Composition over Inheritance'?"* (Because composition couples only through public interfaces, avoids fragile base class breakage, lets you swap behaviors at runtime—Strategy Pattern—and avoids deep rigid hierarchies.)

analogy: Association: a Doctor and Patient interact during an appointment without owning each other's lifetime.
simpleExplanation:
**Association** is the broadest relationship where two independent classes know about and interact with each other (a **"uses-a"** or peer link), with **no ownership** between them. Example: `Doctor` and `Patient`, or `Driver` and `Car` (`driver.drive(car)`).  
  Hierarchy of strength: **Association** (peers interact) -> **Aggregation** (whole contains independent parts) -> **Composition** (whole owns part's lifetime).
definitions: **Association** is the broadest relationship where two independent classes know about and interact with each other (a **"uses-a"** or peer link), with **no ownership** between them. Example: `Doctor` and `Patient`, or `Driver` and `Car` (`driver.drive(car)`).
- **Unidirectional:** Only `Order` holds a pointer/ID to `Customer`; `Customer` doesn't know about `Order`.
interviewTraps: *"Give examples of 1-to-1, 1-to-Many, and Many-to-Many associations."* (1-to-1: `Person`–`Passport`; 1-to-Many: `Teacher`–`Students`; Many-to-Many: `Student`–`Course`.)

*"What consistency bug easily happens with bidirectional associations?"* (Updating one side—adding `course` to `student`—while forgetting to add `student` to `course`, leaving them out of sync. Solve by encapsulating `enroll(Student&, Course&)` in a coordinator/service or a single setter.)

*"In large C++ systems, why do architects often prefer storing IDs (`CourseId`) instead of raw pointers in domain entities?"* (Decoupling, easier serialization to databases/JSON, and zero dangling-pointer risks.)

title: SOLID Principles (Quick Interview Summary)
analogy: SOLID is the 5-rule structural engineering code that keeps a growing software building from collapsing under changes.
simpleExplanation:
- **S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP):** A class should have one clear job (one reason to change).
  - **O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP):** Open for extension (add new behavior), closed for modification (don't rewrite working code).
  - **L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP):** Any `Derived` class must work seamlessly wherever `Base` is expected without breaking expectations.
  - **I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP):** Don't force classes to implement fat interfaces with methods they don't use; split into small focused interfaces.
  - **D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP):** High-level business logic should depend on **abstractions (interfaces)**, not concrete low-level details.
definitions: - **S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP):** A class should have one clear job (one reason to change).

Mathematically, a Square *is-a* Rectangle. In OOP, if `Rectangle` has `setWidth(w)` and `setHeight(h)` that vary independently, and `Square : public Rectangle` overrides both to force `width == height`, then a function testing `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert(r.area() == 20);` **breaks** when given a `Square` (returns 16)! Thus behavioral "is-a" fails, violating LSP. Fix: both inherit from an immutable `Shape { virtual int area() const = 0; }`.
interviewTraps: *"Which SOLID principle directly relies on C++ abstract classes / pure virtual interfaces?"* (OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP all leverage abstractions heavily!)
*"How do you spot an LSP violation in a code review?"* (Derived overrides that throw `NotSupportedException`, leave methods empty `{}`, or strengthen preconditions/weaken postconditions.)

*"In C++, can you apply DIP at compile time without `virtual` functions?"* (Yes! Template policy injection: `template <typename Database> class OrderService`—zero virtual overhead while keeping logic decoupled!)

---
commonMistakes: Translating SRP as *"a class should have only one method"* (false—it means one cohesive responsibility/actor, e.g., `BankAccount` has `deposit`, `withdraw`, `getBalance`, NOT `printPDFInvoice` or `saveToMySQL`).
Assuming real-world taxonomy ("a Penguin is a Bird") always translates directly to C++ inheritance (`Penguin : Bird` where `Bird::fly()` throws an exception—classic LSP violation!).
Confusing Dependency Inversion (the design principle) with Dependency Injection (the technique of passing dependencies via constructor/setter).

title: Rule of 3 / 5 / 0 (Quick Interview Summary)
analogy: Rule of 3/5/0 is resource-ownership discipline: either let smart wrappers manage memory (Rule of 0) or handle all copy/move/destroy rules yourself.
simpleExplanation:
- **Rule of 3 (Pre-C++11):** If a class explicitly needs a custom **Destructor**, **Copy Constructor**, or **Copy Assignment Operator**, it almost certainly manages a raw resource and needs **all three**.
  - **Rule of 5 (C++11+):** Adds **Move Constructor** and **Move Assignment Operator** so temporary objects transfer resources in $O(1)$ instead of expensive deep copies.
  - **Rule of 0 (Modern C++ Best Practice):** Write **none** of those 5 special functions in normal business classes! Instead, delegate resource ownership to RAII wrappers like `std::string`, `std::vector`, and `std::unique_ptr`.
definitions: - **Rule of 3 (Pre-C++11):** If a class explicitly needs a custom **Destructor**, **Copy Constructor**, or **Copy Assignment Operator**, it almost certainly manages a raw resource and needs **all three**.

Writing raw `new`/`delete`, exception-safe copy assignment, self-assignment guards, and `noexcept` move operators manually is error-prone and violates Single Responsibility (mixing business logic with raw memory management). With Rule of 0, a `Student` or `Buffer` using `std::vector<int>` or `std::unique_ptr<T>` gets **correct, leak-free, exception-safe** destruction, copying (or non-copyability), and moving automatically from the compiler!
interviewTraps: *"If you define a custom destructor in a class, what happens to the implicit move constructor?"* (The compiler does NOT generate move operations! Falling back to copy instead of move.)

*"Why should a move constructor and move assignment operator almost always be marked `noexcept`?"* (Because `std::vector` resizing refuses to move elements—and falls back to slow copying—unless the move constructor is `noexcept`, to preserve strong exception safety!)

*"What is the one minor downside of Copy-and-Swap for copy assignment?"* (It always allocates fresh memory for `other` even if `*this` already had enough existing capacity—e.g., `std::vector` reuses existing capacity instead of using copy-and-swap.)

---
commonMistakes: Writing a custom `~MyClass() { delete ptr; }` while leaving default copy constructor/assignment—causing shallow-copy double-free crashes!

Writing empty destructors `~Student() {}` "for good style" in a Rule of 0 class—which accidentally disables the compiler-generated move constructor and move assignment! (If needed for polymorphism, write `virtual ~Base() = default;` and explicitly `= default` or `= delete` copy/move.)
Implementing `swap` using `std::swap(a, b)` inside `Buffer::swap`, which calls assignment and causes infinite recursion! Always swap individual members (`std::swap(a.ptr, b.ptr);`).

title: Copy Assignment Operator
analogy: Copy assignment (`b = a`) is renovating an already-built house to match another house—clearing old furniture safely before copying.
simpleExplanation:
The copy assignment operator (`T& operator=(const T& rhs)`) copies values from an existing object `rhs` into an **already-existing** object `*this`.  
  - `Box b = a;` -> **Copy Constructor** (`b` is being created right now).
  - `b = a;` -> **Copy Assignment Operator** (`b` already existed before this line).
definitions: The copy assignment operator (`T& operator=(const T& rhs)`) copies values from an existing object `rhs` into an **already-existing** object `*this`.

1. **Self-assignment (`a = a;` or `*p = *q;` where `p == q`):** If `operator=` deletes `this->data` before copying `rhs.data`, and `this == &rhs`, it just deleted its own data and now copies garbage! Checking `if (this == &rhs) return *this;` (or copy-and-swap) prevents that disaster.
interviewTraps: *"What does the compiler-generated `operator=` do if you don't write one?"* (Memberwise copy assignment—shallow copy of raw pointers!)
*"Why shouldn't `operator=` return `const T&`?"* (Because `(a = b) = c;` or passing `(a = b)` to a function taking `T&` matches built-in `int` behavior when returning `T&`.)

*"Why is making `operator=` `virtual` in a polymorphic hierarchy generally considered an anti-pattern?"* (Because `Base* p1` and `Base* p2` might point to a `Circle` and a `Square`, and assigning a `Square` into a `Circle` makes no sense!)

---

Writing `void operator=(const T& rhs)` (breaks `a = b = c;`), or deleting `data` before allocating new memory (not exception-safe!).
Forgetting `Base::operator=(rhs);` inside a custom `Derived::operator=`, leaving the `Base` half of `Derived` stale!

questions.question: Why must `operator=` check for self-assignment (`if (this == &rhs) return *this;`) and return `*this` by reference?
questions.answer:
1. **Self-assignment (`a = a;` or `*p = *q;` where `p == q`):** If `operator=` deletes `this->data` before copying `rhs.data`, and `this == &rhs`, it just deleted its own data and now copies garbage! Checking `if (this == &rhs) return *this;` (or copy-and-swap) prevents that disaster.
  2. **Returning `T&` (`*this`):** Allows chained assignment `a = b = c;` (which parses right-to-left as `a.operator=(b.operator=(c))`) without creating unnecessary temporary copies.

questions.question: How does inheritance interact with the Copy Assignment Operator?
questions.answer: If you write a custom `Derived& operator=(const Derived& rhs)`, the compiler will **NOT** automatically copy `Base`'s members! You must explicitly invoke `Base::operator=(rhs);` as the first step inside `Derived::operator=`. Also, if you declare `operator=` in `Base` as `virtual` (rare and usually bad!), beware of slicing/mixed-type assignment bugs.

title: `inline static` Members in C++17
analogy: C++17 `inline static` lets you declare and initialize shared class variables right inside a header without linker headaches.
simpleExplanation:
Before C++17, a normal non-const `static` member like `static int count;` could only be **declared** inside the class—you had to write `int Student::count = 0;` **outside** the class in exactly one `.cpp` file, otherwise you got a linker error (or multiple-definition error if put in a `.h` header included by two `.cpp` files!).  
  C++17 introduced **`inline static int count = 0;`** right inside the class definition—no out-of-class definition needed, and completely safe in header-only libraries!
definitions: Before C++17, a normal non-const `static` member like `static int count;` could only be **declared** inside the class—you had to write `int Student::count = 0;` **outside** the class in exactly one `.cpp` file, otherwise you got a linker error (or multiple-definition error if put in a `.h` header included by two `.cpp` files!).

On a variable (just like on a function), `inline` means **"multiple translation units (`.cpp` files) may see this definition, and the linker will merge them all into ONE single variable in memory without violating the One Definition Rule (ODR)."**
interviewTraps: *"Before C++17, which static members WERE allowed to be initialized directly inside the class?"* (Only `static const` integral/enum types like `static const int MAX = 100;`, and `static constexpr` in C++11+—not `std::string`, `double` pre-C++11, or mutable `int count`!)

*"Are `static constexpr` data members implicitly `inline` in C++17?"* (**Yes!** In C++17, `static constexpr int X = 5;` inside a class is implicitly `inline`—so taking `&MyClass::X` works without needing an out-of-class definition!)

*"Can a class have an `inline static` member of its **own** class type (`inline static Singleton inst;`)?"* (Yes, if defined *out-of-line* or once the class is complete, though inside the class body itself the class is incomplete so `inline static MyClass inst;` directly inside `class MyClass` fails to compile—use `inline` out-of-class or Meyers' Singleton!)
commonMistakes: Thinking `inline static` means *"inlined into every object"* (No! Still **one shared variable** per program for the whole class, just like regular `static`).
Thinking `inline` on a variable is a performance/optimization hint like function inlining (it has nothing to do with speed—it is purely an ODR / linkage rule!).
Assuming `inline static` guarantees cross-TU initialization order (it fixes multiple-definition ODR errors, NOT the Static Initialization Order Fiasco!).
